Read this as a case of remote homology with divergent function, not a case of shared function. In SCOPe, all three domain types sit in the Rossmann-like α/β/α sandwich fold of class c (α/β proteins), the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold fold (c.2). As far as I recall, they are grouped in one superfamily, the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains (c.2.1). Within that superfamily they are placed in separate families: the alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domain family (I believe c.2.1.1), the CoA-binding domain family, and the potassium-channel NAD-binding (RCK/TrkA-like) family. I am not certain of the exact family numbers for the last two, so check them against the SCOPe release you use.

The levels carry different strength. Same superfamily means SCOPe curators judge that structural, and often functional, features such as the βαβ-repeat topology and the dinucleotide-binding mode, support a common evolutionary origin even though sequence identity is low. Separate families mean the sequence similarity and the clearly shared function are too weak to call these close relatives. A same-fold or same-superfamily relationship is therefore evidence for distant ancestry. It is not evidence of the same catalytic chemistry, ligand, or biological role.

The three domains do different things. In alcohol dehydrogenase, the Rossmann C-terminal domain binds NAD(H) and works with a separate GroES-like catalytic domain that binds zinc and the substrate. The catalytic domain is not part of this Rossmann relationship. The CoA-binding domain is a Rossmann-like domain found in CoA-linked enzymes such as the succinyl-CoA synthetase α-subunit. Its ligand preference and role differ from classic NAD(P) dehydrogenases, so do not assume it carries out NAD-dependent redox chemistry. The potassium-channel NAD-binding domain (RCK/TrkA-type) is a regulatory, ligand-sensing domain that controls channel gating. It is not a dehydrogenase, and a bound nucleotide there does not imply redox activity.

Practical interpretation:
- Treat the three as one ancient Rossmann-fold lineage that diversified into different families with different functions.
- Do not transfer enzymatic function, substrate or cofactor specificity, catalytic residues, or regulatory behavior across families on the basis of the shared superfamily alone.
- A Rossmann-like motif such as a GxGxxG loop is not sufficient to predict NAD versus NADP versus CoA binding or any particular activity.
- Use a structural template from one family to model another only for the conserved core fold. Loops, the ligand pocket, and the quaternary or domain context will differ, so check the model with family-specific sequence conservation, ligand-bound structures, and biochemical or mutational evidence.
- When picking a representative structure, choose one from the same family as the query. Do not pick one from the superfamily at large.
- Because this fold is very common, some similarity may come from convergence or from a recurring nucleotide-binding motif. SCOPe's superfamily assignment is an expert judgment, not a statistical proof, and it can change between releases.

In short, the SCOPe relationship tells you the three domains share a Rossmann-fold ancestry. It does not tell you they share a function.
